headline: What the biggest voices in bonds are saying
bigPicture: The shared view among the market’s leading voices is that the era of cheap money is over. The Federal Reserve raised rates in September because inflation has been above its 2% goal for more than five years, and minutes released Oct 7 show most officials expect another hike by year end. The 10-year Treasury yield has climbed above 5.3%, its highest level since 2002.

The pressure comes from supply as much as inflation. Federal debt has passed $40 trillion, the government keeps borrowing heavily, and traditional foreign buyers such as Japan and China are buying fewer Treasuries. Several of these investors say that makes buy-and-hold in long-term bonds riskier than it used to be.

They are not all bearish on bonds. BlackRock’s Rick Rieder and PIMCO see today’s yields as an opportunity, especially in high-quality and shorter-term bonds, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says the rise is a global trend rather than a U.S. problem. Gundlach, Dalio and Druckenmiller warn that long-term Treasuries may not protect investors in the next downturn the way they used to.
agree: Rates will stay higher for longer
Government debt is the core pressure on yields
Quality matters more than chasing extra yield
differ: Long-term Treasuries are starting to look worth owning
PIMCO, Capital Group, and Rieder (in small amounts)
Long-term Treasuries may not be a safe haven next time

voices.name: Kevin Warsh
voices.where: FOMC statement, press conference and meeting minutes
points: The Fed raised its target range to 3.75%–4.00% in a unanimous 12–0 vote, citing inflation that has run above target for more than five years.

He gave no promise about further hikes, but the meeting minutes released Oct 7 show most officials think another increase would likely be appropriate by year end, citing too little recent progress on inflation.

He linked the rise in long-term yields to a strong economy, heavy corporate investment competing for capital, and geopolitical uncertainty, and said the Fed does not need to hurt the job market to succeed.
voices.quote: The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long.

voices.name: Scott Bessent
points: He played down the jump in yields, describing it as part of a global rise in borrowing costs rather than a U.S.-specific problem.
He said he would worry about a rise unique to the U.S., and that investors are not selling Treasuries to buy German or Japanese bonds.
He acknowledged the limits of his role, saying he cannot control the bond market but can urge people to slow down and think.
voices.quote: I can’t control the bond market.

voices.name: Mohamed El-Erian
points: He expects the global government-bond selloff to run further, because traditional big buyers of Treasuries, notably Japan and China, have been buying less. On Oct 1 he said upward pressure on yields remains the dominant theme.
He sees the core problem as a fiscal imbalance with no political appetite to fix it, which keeps upward pressure on borrowing costs for households and businesses.
He also cautions that investors anchored to a decade of ultra-low yields may be reacting to today’s levels with more fear than the fundamentals justify.
voices.quote: It has much more to do with fundamental imbalance than inflation or Fed credibility.

voices.name: Jeffrey Gundlach
voices.where: CNBC; interview with David Rosenberg, reported by MarketWatch
points: He said the Fed should have raised rates by half a point, not a quarter, given its own forecast that inflation won’t reach 2% until 2029.

He warned that the next recession could push long-term Treasury yields up rather than down, and on Oct 1 added that the dollar may fall rather than rise next time, as heavy government debt leaves only inflationary ways out.
He called the U.S. stock market a hollow tree: the index looks healthy only because a handful of giant companies are holding it up while most stocks have fallen well off their highs.
voices.quote: Long-term rates are going to go up because of the debt crisis…

voices.name: Ray Dalio
points: He warned that interest costs on U.S. debt, now above $40 trillion, are crowding out other spending, and that rising yields and weaker foreign demand make the path riskier.
He put the timing of a U.S. debt crisis at roughly three years, give or take two, if nothing changes.
His suggested response is broad diversification: hold fewer bonds than usual and keep a meaningful slice in gold.
voices.quote: It will come in three years, give or take two…

voices.name: Stanley Druckenmiller
points: He criticized the Treasury’s plan to buy back bonds to hold yields down, arguing that yields reflect growth, deficits and debt, not something policy can wish away.
He sees rising rates as a warning signal that disciplines government borrowing, and says muting that signal makes the danger worse.
His fix is to cut the deficit rather than manage bond prices.
voices.quote: Governments defending prices against fundamentals always lose.

voices.name: Rick Rieder
voices.role: CIO of Global Fixed Income, BlackRock
points: He has turned more cautious on U.S. stocks because high-quality bonds now pay enough to be a real alternative.
He favors short-term, high-quality bonds at the front of the curve and has started adding a little in long-term Treasuries.
He warns that every 1-point rise in rates adds about $100 billion a year to government interest costs, which eventually has to pull rates back down.
voices.quote: We're going to have a compounding debt problem in the country.

voices.name: Dan Ivascyn
points: PIMCO has been buying mortgage-backed and asset-backed bonds, sees company bonds as expensive, and trimmed its bet against long-term U.S. bonds once yields topped 5%.
Other large managers, including Vanguard, PGIM, Fidelity and Capital Group, are also leaning toward high-quality, shorter-term bonds and mortgage bonds, and are picky about AI-related debt.
He describes a market with a wider range of possible outcomes than usual.
voices.quote: Fatter tails, more extreme potential outcomes.

actions: Keep an emergency fund that earns
Hold 3 to 6 months of essential expenses in a high-yield savings account, money-market fund or Treasury bills. At today’s rates, cash is earning around 4%.
The Fed just raised rates, and credit cards and home-equity lines reset with it. Paying them down is a guaranteed return.
Match bonds to when you need the money
Money needed in the next few years belongs in short-term bonds or a ladder of Treasuries that mature when you need them, not in long-term bond funds.
Duration tells you roughly how much a fund falls when yields rise 1 point. A fund with a 15-year duration can lose about 15%. The Bonds page shows this for any Treasury.
Most of these managers prefer Treasuries, investment-grade and mortgage bonds over high-yield debt right now. Chasing a little more income can mean taking a lot more risk.
Spread savings across stocks, bonds and cash, consider inflation-protected Treasuries (TIPS) for part of your bond money, and keep automatic investing on rather than trying to time the market.
